blocks.text: 10.4.2. Custom Annotation Creation
A support agent with no roles voided a customer's payment. The method is guarded:

@Role("ADMIN") @Role("AUDITOR")
public void voidPayment() { }

and the guard, written when every method had one role, reads `getAnnotation(Role.class)` and lets the call through when it finds no `@Role`. `refund()`, which carries a single `@Role("ADMIN")`, refuses the same agent. Both methods compile, but javac stores their annotations differently.

Every annotation this page reads by reflection is `@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)`; what the other retentions keep is unit 10.4.3. Reading annotations inside javac with a processor is unit 10.4.4, and the built-in ones such as `@Override` are unit 10.4.1.
An Element Holds a Compile-Time Constant of a Few Types
An annotation type is declared with `@interface`. Which of these elements compile?

Cache.java:7: error: element value must be a constant expression
    String owner() default null;                         // 4
                           ^
Cache.java:8: error: expression not allowed as annotation value
    long ttlMillis() default System.currentTimeMillis(); // 5
                                                     ^
Cache.java:4: error: invalid type for annotation interface element
    Object key();                                        // 1
    ^
Cache.java:5: error: invalid type for annotation interface element
    List<String> regions();                              // 2
        ^
Cache.java:6: error: invalid type for annotation interface element
    Integer maxEntries();                                // 3
    ^
Cache.java:9: error: invalid type for annotation interface element
    String[][] tiers();                                  // 6
          ^
6 errors

None compiles. An element's type is a primitive, `String`, `Class`, an enum, another annotation, or a one-dimensional array of one of these. Every value, the defaults included, is fixed when javac runs: the class file stores it as a constant, an enum constant's name, a class name, a nested annotation or an array of these, so the JVM can rebuild it without calling the code that computed it. A `List`, an `Integer` or a call has no such form. `null` has none either, so "not set" needs a sentinel: `""`, `-1`, or `Void.class` for a `Class` element.
The value must be a constant expression in the language's sense, and a `static final` field is not always one:

Retry.java:10: error: element value must be a constant expression
    int fromEnv() default Limits.FROM_ENV;        // error
                                ^
Retry.java:11: error: element value must be a constant expression
    int boxed() default Limits.BOXED;             // error
                              ^
2 errors

A team that wants the retry count to come from configuration can't put it in the annotation, as a default or at the use site. The annotation names a key (`@Retry(attemptsKey = "orders.retries")`), and the code that reads the annotation looks the value up.
Defaults Live in the Annotation Type, and Only value Can Go Unnamed
A small web library declares `@Endpoint`, and a service uses it:

list: @Endpoint(method="GET", produces={"application/json"}, timeoutMs=2000, value="/orders")
  GET /orders, timeout 2000 ms
export: @Endpoint(method="POST", produces={"text/csv"}, timeoutMs=2000, value="/orders")
  POST /orders, timeout 2000 ms
`getAnnotation` returns an object of the annotation type; each element call returns the use-site value or the default. A single value for an array element needs no braces (`produces = "text/csv"`).
Now the library's next release lowers the default to `int timeoutMs() default 500;`. We recompile `Endpoint.java` alone and run the same `Orders.class`:

list: @Endpoint(method="GET", produces={"application/json"}, timeoutMs=500, value="/orders")
  GET /orders, timeout 500 ms
export: @Endpoint(method="POST", produces={"text/csv"}, timeoutMs=500, value="/orders")
  POST /orders, timeout 500 ms

The class file of `Orders` records only the elements written at the use site. The default is stored once, in `Endpoint.class`, and filled in when the annotation is read. Upgrading the library jar changes the timeout of every endpoint that didn't set one, with no rebuild of the service, so a changed default belongs in the release notes.

`@Endpoint("/orders")` leaves out the name `value`. That is the only element whose name may go, and only when every other element has a default. Declare `@Endpoint` with no default for `method`, and the shorthand fails:

Endpoint.java:7: error: annotation @Endpoint is missing a default value for the element 'method'
    @Endpoint("/users")
    ^
1 error
@Target Is Checked by javac at Every Use
A timing aspect wraps methods annotated `@Timed`, and someone writes `@Timed` on a field. With `@Target(ElementType.METHOD)`, javac refuses it:

Timed.java:8: error: annotation interface not applicable to this kind of declaration
    @Timed
    ^
1 error

Without `@Target`, the field compiles, the aspect never looks at fields, and nothing is timed. An annotation type with no `@Target` is accepted on every declaration, a type parameter included, and in no type context:

Tag.java:7: error: annotation @Tag not applicable in this type context
    List<@Tag String> ids;
         ^
1 error
Annotations written on a type, such as `List<@NonNull String>`, need `ElementType.TYPE_USE` in the target.
A Repeated Annotation Is Stored Inside Its Container
The opening's service and its guard:

refund, support agent allowed: false
voidPayment, support agent allowed: true

refund:
  getAnnotation(Role.class)          @Repeat.Role("ADMIN")
  getAnnotation(Roles.class)         null
  getAnnotationsByType(Role.class)   [@Repeat.Role("ADMIN")]
  getAnnotations()                   [@Repeat.Role("ADMIN")]
voidPayment:
  getAnnotation(Role.class)          null
  getAnnotation(Roles.class)         @Repeat.Roles({@Repeat.Role("ADMIN"), @Repeat.Role("AUDITOR")})
  getAnnotationsByType(Role.class)   [@Repeat.Role("ADMIN"), @Repeat.Role("AUDITOR")]
  getAnnotations()                   [@Repeat.Roles({@Repeat.Role("ADMIN"), @Repeat.Role("AUDITOR")})]

`@Repeatable(Roles.class)` lets you write `@Role` more than once. When you do, javac writes a single `@Roles({@Role("ADMIN"), @Role("AUDITOR")})` into the class file instead (`javap -v` shows only `Roles` on `voidPayment`), and no `@Role` is directly on the method. `getAnnotation(Role.class)` returns `null`, and the guard opened the method to anyone. A single `@Role` is stored as itself, so `getAnnotation(Roles.class)` is `null` there. Code that reads only the container breaks on the other half of the methods.
`getAnnotationsByType(Role.class)` looks through the container and returns every `@Role` in the order written, for one or for many, so code that reads a repeatable annotation should use it.

javac checks the container against the repeatable annotation, among other rules: it needs a `value()` element of the repeatable type's array, a retention at least as long, and targets that are a subset of the repeatable type's. Forget its `@Retention`, and it defaults to `CLASS`:

Role.java:4: error: retention of containing annotation interface (Roles) is shorter than the retention of repeatable annotation interface (Role)
@Repeatable(Roles.class)
^
1 error

@Inherited Reaches a Class Only from Its Superclasses
An audit interceptor logs every call to a class carrying `@Audited` and reads the level from it:

CardService    getAnnotation: @Inherit.Audited(level="BASIC")      getDeclaredAnnotation: @Inherit.Audited(level="BASIC")
StripeService  getAnnotation: @Inherit.Audited(level="BASIC")      getDeclaredAnnotation: null
LedgerService  getAnnotation: null                                 getDeclaredAnnotation: null
StripeService.pay() getAnnotation: null
StripeService @Owner: null

`StripeService` declares nothing and still gets `BASIC`. When a class has no `@Audited` of its own, `getAnnotation` asks its superclass, then that one's superclass, and returns the first it finds, so the nearest declaration wins and `FULL` two levels up is never seen. `getDeclaredAnnotation` skips that search. `@Owner` has no `@Inherited`, so it stays on `BaseService`.

`LedgerService` implements an audited interface and isn't audited: the `@Inherited` javadoc says annotations on implemented interfaces have no effect. `StripeService.pay()` overrides an audited method and isn't audited either: `@Inherited` has no effect on anything but a class, even though `Audited` allows `METHOD`. A developer who overrides `pay()` to add a log line has removed its auditing.

A superclass chain has one nearest declaration; a class can implement two interfaces that carry different values. A library that wants interface or method annotations walks the hierarchy in its own code, with its own rule for which declaration wins.

Summary

items: **An element holds a compile-time constant** of a primitive, `String`, `Class`, enum, annotation or a one-dimensional array of these. No `null`, no collections, nothing computed at run time: configuration can't reach an annotation.

**Defaults live in the annotation type** and are filled in when the annotation is read, so a library that changes a default changes every caller that didn't set it. Only `value` may be written unnamed, and only when every other element has a default.
**`@Target` is checked by javac at every use.** Without it, a misplaced annotation compiles and is silently ignored by whatever reads it.
**A repeated annotation is stored inside its container.** `getAnnotation(Role.class)` misses a repeated `@Role`, and a guard that reads it opens the method; `getAnnotationsByType` finds every one.
**`@Inherited` reaches a class only from its superclasses**, nearest first. Interfaces, methods and fields inherit nothing.

blocks.text: Challenges

items: A security library must decide whether a method with no `@Role` is open or closed. Which default would have made the opening's bug fail safe, and what would it cost a team adopting the library on an existing code base?
You need `@Endpoint` timeouts to differ between staging and production. Design the annotation and its reader so that no value is compiled into a class file.

Write a lookup that finds `@Audited` on an interface method when the implementing method has none. Decide what it does when two interfaces disagree, and when a superclass method disagrees with an interface.

blocks.text: Design Note: Annotations Are Constants So the JVM Can Read Them Without Running Code

The element rules on this page follow from one choice: an annotation's values live in the class file as constants. Reflection rebuilds an annotation from those bytes, a processor reads them before the program exists, and a tool can read them from the class files without loading a class.

The cost is that an annotation can't express anything that is decided later: an environment's timeout, a role list from a database, `null`. Those end up as keys and sentinels that some other code resolves, and the annotation then states only part of what happens. The default is the exception: it is looked up in the annotation type when the annotation is read, which is why an upgrade can change it without a rebuild.
